title: Measuring Verifier Impact in an LLM Generate→Verify→Repair Loop for Intent→Configuration NetOps Tasks
abstract: We measure how inserting a deterministic network verifier into a generate→verify→repair (G→V→R) loop affects verifier-detected safety violations for LLM-produced device-configuration proposals. In a preregistered paired design (N = 500 intent→configuration tasks stratified across VLAN-change, ACL-change, and static-route-change clusters) we compared: (1) baseline — a single LLM proposal produced once per task, and (2) guarded — the identical shared LLM proposal validated by a deterministic netops verifier and subjected to up to one automated repair iteration if the verifier flagged a preregistered high/medium-severity violation. Primary outcome: verifier pass (no preregistered high/medium-severity violations). Results (complete pairs = 500): baseline passed 499/500 (0.998), guarded passed 500/500 (1.000); contingency: n11 = 499, n10 = 1, n01 = 0, n00 = 0. Absolute paired success-rate difference (guarded − baseline) = 0.002; paired-bootstrap 95% percentile CI = [0.0, 0.006] (B = 10,000, seed = 1729). The preregistered exact McNemar two-sided test was implemented as an exact binomial on discordant pairs (n = n10 + n01) with two-sided p computed as 2·min{P(X ≤ n10), P(X ≥ n10)} for X∼Binomial(n,0.5); for the observed discordant counts this yields p = 1.00 under the archived executor convention. Interpretation: on this verifier-scoped synthetic corpus and model+validator pairing the LLM produced near-ceiling proposals; measured marginal verifier+repair effect on the pass-rate metric is therefore small, though the verifier corrected at least one concrete baseline failure. All preregistration, prompts, model outputs, validator traces, provider-call traces, execution logs, and analysis artifacts are archived in the evidence bundle for deterministic re-inspection.

sections.introduction:
Generative large language models (LLMs) are rapidly being applied to NetOps tasks such as intent-to-configuration translation, multi-step change planning, and automated repair. Prior system reports and surveys emphasize that operational safety depends heavily on surrounding engineering—deterministic validators, sandbox replay, canarying, and rollback mechanisms—which motivates generate→verify→repair (G→V→R) architectures that place a verifier between generation and execution [Beckett et al., 2017; Wei et al., 2025; Bilal et al., 2026].

Despite that conceptual consensus, there are few controlled measurements that isolate the marginal contribution of a verifier when the LLM’s proposal is held fixed. Practically, operators must know: when an LLM already produces high-quality candidates for a verifier-modeled property set, how much incremental safety does adding a verifier plus a modest automated repair budget provide on a verifier-scoped pass/fail metric? To address this, we preregistered and executed a paired experiment that isolates verifier+repair impact under canonical, deterministic semantics. Our research question: given identical initial proposals (shared_initial_candidate semantics), how much does integrating a deterministic verifier and at most one automated repair iteration reduce verifier-detected safety violations compared to the same LLM alone? The paper reports the preregistered design, execution accounting, confirmatory analysis, and artifact-grounded diagnostics.
sections.related_work:
Formal deterministic verification methods (header-space analysis, route-model verifiers, Batfish-style analyzers) provide machine-checkable properties such as reachability, isolation, and update atomicity; these methods are well established and motivate verifier-in-the-loop system designs [Beckett et al., 2017]. Concurrently, recent NetOps/AIOps systems and intent-translation research demonstrate LLM integrations for configuration generation while advocating operational guardrails (e.g., INTA, Confucius, other agentic NetOps frameworks) [INTA, 2025; Wang et al., 2025; Bilal et al., 2026]. Generate–verify–repair patterns appear across structured-generation domains as a means to reduce unsafe or incorrect outputs (methodological proposals and select instantiations are available in the literature) [PoeTone; INTA].

Separately, studies of LLM failure modes (hallucination, overconfidence, tool-integration errors) argue for verification or human oversight as mitigations [Owen, 2026; DeepSeek-AI, 2025]. What is less prevalent is a preregistered ablation that quantifies the marginal verifier effect while keeping the LLM’s initial output identical for both arms. This study contributes such an artifact-backed measurement and situates it with the nearest system and verification literature.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and confirmatory plan. We preregistered study_id cand_7f4b9a2d_hosted_gvr_v1_2026, freezing the research question, task generator seeds, strata, inclusion/exclusion rules, estimands, analysis executor, multiplicity plan, retry policy, and stopping rule prior to execution. Primary confirmatory hypothesis: an LLM paired with a deterministic verifier plus a single automated repair iteration will produce a lower verifier-detected safety-violation rate than the same LLM producing a single proposal without verifier feedback (paired within-task). Primary estimand: paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline where success == verifier reports zero preregistered high/medium-severity violations. The preregistration and artifacts are archived (preregistration SHA-256 recorded in the execution manifest).

Task generation and stratification. A deterministic synthetic corpus of 500 intent→configuration tasks was generated with deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5 using preregistered seeds and the preregistered stratification across three clusters. The executed per-cluster allocation matched the preregistered plan: VLAN-change = 167 tasks, ACL-change = 167 tasks, static-route-change = 166 tasks (complete_pair_count = 500). The generator constrained allowed_features to {admin, mtu, vlan} to match the deterministic verifier’s modeled scope; the full task manifest (inputs, seeds, expected_final_state, required_sequence) is archived under execution/task_manifest.jsonl. No confirmatory exclusions occurred in this run.

Generation semantics and experimental control. To isolate verifier+repair effect we used generation_semantics = "shared_initial_candidate" (independent_condition_generation = false): for each task the pipeline produced a single shared LLM proposal; that identical candidate served as the baseline output and was also validated by the guarded arm. The guarded path invoked the automated single-repair call only if the deterministic verifier reported a preregistered high/medium-severity violation on the shared candidate. This choice prevents conflation with verifier-guided regeneration and isolates the effect of verification plus at most one repair applied to the same initial proposal.

Models, adapter, and verifier. Requested LLM = gpt-5-mini called via the hosted_netops_gvr_v1 adapter (provider recorded as openai_responses); model configuration is archived (execution/model_configuration.json). The deterministic verifier used for gating and scoring was deterministic_netops_validator_v5; the validator-spec and violation-code→severity mapping are archived in the evidence bundle. The guarded arm permitted at most one automated repair iteration per preregistration.

Statistical inference and exact test implementation. The preregistered confirmatory test is an exact McNemar two-sided test on paired binary outcomes. Our archived executor implements the two-sided test by forming the number of discordant pairs n = n10 + n01 and performing an exact binomial test on the observed n10 (the count of pairs where guarded passes and baseline fails) under X∼Binomial(n,0.5). The two-sided p-value is computed as p_two-sided = 2·min{P(X ≤ n10), P(X ≥ n10)} (truncated at 1.0). This exact-binomial-on-discordant-pairs convention and the analysis code path are recorded in analysis/analysis_log.jsonl and analysis artifacts. We also compute paired-bootstrap percentile 95% CIs for the absolute difference (B = 10,000, bootstrap_seed = 1729) with pairing preserved.
sections.results:
Execution accounting and primary outcomes. The run completed with complete_pair_count = 500 and model_calls_used = 501 (shared_initial_generation = 500; repair-stage calls observed = 1). Aggregate counts (analysis/condition_summary.csv): baseline successes = 499, baseline failures = 1 (baseline_success_rate = 0.998); guarded successes = 500, guarded failures = 0 (guarded_success_rate = 1.000). Paired contingency (guarded × baseline): n11 = 499, n10 = 1, n01 = 0, n00 = 0 (analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv). Absolute paired success-rate difference (guarded − baseline) = 0.002.

Exact McNemar two-sided p-value and CI. Applying the archived exact-binomial-on-discordant-pairs convention (n = 1, n10 = 1) yields p = 1.00 under the executor’s two-sided rule; paired-bootstrap percentile 95% CI for the absolute difference is [0.0, 0.006] (B = 10,000, seed = 1729). All analysis artifacts and parameters are archived in analysis/* in the evidence bundle.

Discordant episode provenance and repair trace. Exactly one repair-stage provider call occurred and it produced the sole discordant outcome (the single pair where guarded converted a baseline failure into a verified pass). The run archive contains the deterministic pair identifier and full per-task validator_trace and repair_provider_trace for that episode; these are recorded in execution/raw_results.jsonl and the execution task manifest. To preserve artifact integrity in the paper while enabling deterministic audit, readers can locate the discordant episode by filtering execution/raw_results.jsonl for entries with baseline pass==0 and guarded pass==1 (this lookup deterministically returns the single episode). The archived validator_trace for that episode records the violation class and the repair prompt/response; the repair-stage provider-call trace is archived alongside it. (The execution manifest and deterministic_reconciliation.json confirm model_calls_used = 501 and repair-stage calls = 1.)

Power and ceiling effects. The preregistered power calculation assumed baseline error prevalence ≈ 0.30; observed baseline failure prevalence (1/500) was far lower, creating a ceiling effect that reduces sensitivity to detect small absolute improvements. Consequently, secondary per-violation-class analyses were uninformative due to near-zero counts. Diagnostics (missingness_summary.csv, contamination_summary.csv, deterministic_reconciliation.json) indicate no exclusions, no contamination flags, and zero failed episodes under the execution contract.
sections.discussion:
Operational interpretation. Under the constrained experimental regime—single requested model (gpt-5-mini), shared-initial_candidate semantics, deterministic verifier coverage limited to allowed_fields = {admin, mtu, vlan}, and at most one automated repair iteration—the LLM produced near-ceiling correct proposals and the marginal measured pass-rate benefit of adding the verifier was small (0.002). This is a conditional, verifier-scoped result: when baseline proposal quality is very high on the verifier-modeled properties, a modest verifier+repair budget may yield negligible measured gains on a composite pass/fail metric, although the verifier can still correct rare concrete failures (as the single repaired episode demonstrates).

Design implications. The shared_initial_candidate semantics intentionally isolate verifier+repair effect conditional on identical proposals and are operationally relevant when regeneration costs must be minimized or when preserving the original proposal for human review is required. Alternative operational choices—verifier-guided regeneration, multiple repair iterations, or richer repair objectives—may yield larger effect sizes and should be evaluated under separate preregistrations.

Threats to validity. Internal validity is supported by preregistration, deterministic seeding, and automated replacement rules; no manual adjudication occurred. Construct validity is limited by verifier coverage: the pass==no high/medium violation outcome is defined relative to the validator’s modeled property set and severity mapping (archived in the validator-spec). External validity is limited by single-model testing, synthetic tasks, and constrained feature scope; results do not establish cross-vendor or multi-model generality.

Statistical nuance. The archived exact McNemar two-sided p = 1.00 reflects the executor’s exact-binomial-on-discordant-pairs computation and the empirical discordant counts (n = 1). With very small n, exact two-sided p-values can be non-intuitive; the paired-bootstrap CI provides complementary uncertainty quantification. Together they indicate a small point estimate (0.002) but limited inferential resolution due to a ceiling effect.
sections.conclusion: We conducted a preregistered, artifact-backed paired experiment (N = 500) that isolated the verifier+single-repair effect under shared_initial_candidate semantics. The LLM produced near-ceiling verifier-scoped proposals (baseline 499/500; guarded 500/500), yielding an absolute improvement of 0.002 (95% CI [0.0, 0.006]; archived exact McNemar two-sided p = 1.00 under the run’s exact-binomial convention). This conditional measurement illustrates a ceiling-effect regime: when baseline proposal quality is very high for verifier-modeled properties and verifier coverage is limited, the measurable marginal pass-rate benefit of a modest verifier+repair budget can be negligible on a composite pass/fail metric, although the verifier can still correct rare concrete failures. Practitioners should measure baseline error prevalence on representative workloads, align verifier coverage with operator-critical properties, and select generation/repair semantics that match deployment priorities. All preregistration, inputs, prompts, model outputs, validator traces, provider-call logs, execution manifests, and analysis artifacts are archived in the evidence bundle for deterministic re-inspection.

limitations: Synthetic, deterministic task corpus limited to features modeled by the deterministic validator; task payloads constrained to allowed_fields = {admin, mtu, vlan}. Results do not generalize to unconstrained production intents, cross-vendor CLI heterogeneity, or protocol semantics outside the verifier scope.
Single requested model family (gpt-5-mini requested) and a single validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5) — no claim of multi-model or cross-validator generality is made.
Maximum one automated repair iteration was permitted by the preregistration; different repair budgets or iterative regeneration strategies could change measured verifier impact.

Very high baseline pass rate (499/500) created a ceiling effect that limits power to detect small absolute improvements on the pass-rate metric; the archived exact McNemar two-sided p = 1.00 reflects the archived exact-binomial-on-discordant-pairs convention and the small discordant count.

The single discordant episode (the sole task where baseline failed and guarded succeeded) and its validator diagnostics and repair-stage trace are archived in execution/raw_results.jsonl in the evidence bundle. To inspect it deterministically: filter execution/raw_results.jsonl for pair entries where the baseline scoring outcome indicates a preregistered high/medium-severity violation (baseline pass == 0) while the guarded scoring outcome indicates pass == 1; because only one such discordant pair exists in the confirmatory set, this lookup returns the single episode and its provider-call traces. The validator violation-code→severity mapping is archived in the execution manifest and validator-spec artifacts in the bundle.
